title: Roll a knife and fork up in a cloth napkin
instruction: Roll the knife and fork up in the white napkin.
context: Rolling silverware is side work in almost every table-service restaurant: O*NET lists it for waiters and waitresses (35-3031.00: "Roll silverware, set up food stations, or set up dining areas to prepare for the next shift or for large parties"), an occupation of 2.28 million US jobs (O*NET OnLine, employment 2025). It is hard for a robot in ways a rigid pick-and-place task is not. The napkin is limp cloth lying flat, so it can only be taken by an edge once that edge hangs over the table. The knife and fork are loose inside it and have to stay together. And the bundle has to be let go and taken again while it is half rolled, when it would rather roll back. A roll that is loose, or leaves a piece outside, falls apart when it is carried to the table and is done again; cutlery that ends up on the bare table is no longer clean for a guest.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the main table: x forward (away from the robot), y to the robot's left; heights above the main table. Side table (fixed, wood): a top 50 x 84 x 2 cm spanning x 22 to 72, y -42 to +42, its upper surface 20 cm up, smooth (friction 0.2); it stands on two 2 cm leg boards across its width at x 30 to 32 and x 68 to 70. Napkin (loose, white cloth): one sheet 23.5 x 28 cm, 2.5 mm thick, 68 g (a 47 x 56 cm dinner napkin folded in quarters), lying flat on the side table, centred on y 0, its near edge at x 22.5 and its far edge at x 46. Table knife (loose, steel, 85 g): 24 cm long, 2.05 cm wide, 0.7 cm thick, lying on the side table left of the napkin, parallel to the near edge, centre at x 26, y 27.5, handle to the robot's left. Dinner fork (loose, steel, 45 g): 19.5 cm long, 2.5 cm wide, 1.3 cm high (arched), lying on the side table right of the napkin, parallel to the near edge, centre at x 26, y -25.25, handle to the robot's left. Nothing else is on either table. One layout; run with object_jitter=0.
scoring: Measured on the last step from the napkin's 1,435 mesh nodes and the knife's and fork's poses. Score 0 unless all of these hold: the knife, the fork and the napkin are on the side table (knife and fork centres over its top and between 0.5 cm below and 8 cm above it; no part of the napkin more than 10 cm below it); the fork lies along the knife (fork centre within 3 cm of the knife's centre line, and within 20 degrees of it); the napkin goes all the way round both (at 9 stations over the middle 80% of each piece, napkin within 3.5 cm on every side with no gap of 120 degrees or more, at 75% or more of the stations); and the napkin goes at least 0.9 times round the knife (winding of the napkin's cross-section about the knife's axis, at the middle of the handle; lying open under the knife it is 0.5). Then: 0.3 if it goes 0.9 to under 1.15 times round (folded over); 0.6 if 1.15 or more (rolled on); 0.8 if 1.6 or more and the napkin is at most 11 cm wide across the knife (rolled up; it starts 23.5 cm). 1.0 only if it is rolled up and let go: the roll lies on the side table (knife and fork centres at most 4 cm above its top) and every finger pad of both grippers has been at least 2 cm from the napkin, the knife and the fork for the last 2 s. A rolled-up bundle still held, pressed on or lifted scores 0.8. The trial ends with 1.0 once the score is 1.0 and the knife and fork have moved under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s for 2 s. Doing nothing scores 0.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Unroll the napkin and lay it flat on its marks, its near edge 0.5 cm in from the side table's near edge; lay the knife and the fork back on their marks.
fidelity: The napkin is true cloth (a PhysX deformable surface, 1,435 nodes), not rigid pieces: one sheet with the size, thickness and weight of a dinner napkin folded in quarters. It is limp but springier than cotton and does not cling to itself. The knife and fork are rigid steel shapes of our own making. Gripper pads hold cloth by friction alone, which creeps under load. The side table's top is smooth (friction 0.2), so the napkin slides on it readily.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 after 3,000 steps (termination: step limit); scripted demo: 1.0 after 2,088 steps
